issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Kiet had always taken pride in his work as a carpenter, carefully measuring each cut and sanding every surface until it was smooth. But that attention to detail began to slip after the night he was stopped by police on his way home from a late shift. He remembered the flashing lights, the shouting officers, and the feeling of being slammed against the hood of the car. Kiet's mind replayed the events of that night over and over, but with each iteration, he became more convinced that it was all his fault - if only he had pulled over sooner, if only he had kept his hands visible. The self-blame seeped into every aspect of his life, making him withdrawn and isolated. He stopped going out with friends, stopped taking on new projects at work, and even stopped leaving the house unless absolutely necessary. His wife, Linh, tried to be supportive, but Kiet could sense her frustration growing as he became increasingly distant. To cope with the constant anxiety, Kiet started using marijuana more frequently, hoping it would calm his racing thoughts. But the relief was short-lived, and soon he found himself relying on it just to get through each day. One of the few places where Kiet felt somewhat at ease was in crowded restaurants or cafes - as long as he could position himself with his back against a wall, where he could see everyone around him. He rationalized that this way, no one could sneak up behind him, and he would always have an escape route if needed. When out running errands or waiting in line, Kiet became easily agitated by delays, assuming the worst-case scenario - that someone was trying to harm him or Linh. Even simple tasks like grocery shopping turned into exercises in threat assessment. Kiet's inability to relax even in safe spaces began to take a toll on his relationships and daily life. He would wake up multiple times during the night, drenched in sweat, with visions of police cars chasing him through the streets. At work, he found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats, making it difficult to focus on his tasks. His hands, once steady and confident, now trembled as he tried to drive nails into wood. Linh grew increasingly worried about Kiet's condition, trying to coax him out of the house or get him to talk about what was bothering him. But every conversation ended with Kiet retreating further into himself, convinced that he was failing her, and everyone else around him. The drugs didn't help; they just masked the symptoms temporarily. It wasn't until Kiet's boss called him into the office, concerned about his declining performance and increasing absences, that Kiet realized something needed to change. He knew he couldn't keep living in this constant state of hypervigilance, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. The fear that finally propelled him to seek help was not just the loss of his job or the strain on his marriage but the terror of losing himself entirely - becoming a shadow of the man he once was. As Kiet sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with the worn hem of his jeans, he knew it wouldn't be easy. But maybe, just maybe, talking about what happened that night and the fears that followed would help him find a way back to himself - away from the cycle of self-blame and anxiety that had become his life.
